title: One request
intro: An application asks a server to do something. The server runs the work and returns a response. Here the request asks for a user profile.
takeaway: A request is the ask. A response is the result. The server does work between them.
question: What is the server doing while the application waits?
answer: It is processing the request. The response travels back only after that work finishes.

title: Share the work
intro: A server has finite capacity. A second server can run the same service, so separate requests can be handled at the same time. This simplified example gives each server one work slot.
takeaway: More servers can provide more capacity when requests can be handled independently. Someone still needs to choose a server.
question: Does adding a second server make one request run twice as fast?
answer: No. Here it lets two separate requests run at once. Each request still takes its own processing time.

beats.text: Two servers can run the same service.
The first request starts on server A.
A second request starts on server B while A works.

title: Take turns
intro: A load balancer receives a request and selects a server. Round robin is a selection rule: take turns between eligible servers. Here both servers have the same configured weight.
takeaway: Round robin rotates through servers: A, B, A, B. A request goes to one selected server.
question: After A, B, A, which server gets the next request?
answer: B, provided both servers remain eligible and equally weighted.

beats.text: The rule repeats A, B, A, B.

title: Unequal work
intro: Taking turns balances the number of assigned requests, but requests can take different amounts of work. Watch a slow report on A and a short lookup on B. This example allows one running request per server.
takeaway: Equal request counts do not imply equal remaining work. Round robin can choose a busy server even while another is idle.
question: Why does request 3 wait even though B is ready?
answer: The round-robin rule selects A next. In this one-slot example A is still working, so the new request waits there.

beats.text: B is ready while A remains busy.
Round robin selects A and request 3 waits.
A finishes and the waiting request starts.

title: Look at active work
intro: Another rule is least requests: choose a server with fewer requests still in progress. We start with the same imbalance as before: A has one long-running request and B has none. Counts are useful signals, not perfect measurements of cost.
takeaway: Least requests uses current active-request counts when choosing where new work goes. It does not move existing work.
question: Does choosing B move the long-running request away from A?
answer: No. A keeps its existing request. Only the new request goes to B.

beats.text: A has one active request; B has none.
The new request goes to B.

title: Avoid a failed server
intro: A selection rule also needs to know which servers are eligible. In this example a periodic health probe gets no successful response from A. After its configured timeout, the balancer marks A unavailable and sends new requests to B.
takeaway: Health checks can remove a failed server from new routing decisions after detection. They do not instantly detect every failure or rescue requests already sent.
question: If A fails just after a successful check, is the failure detected immediately?
answer: No. Detection depends on the next checks, their timeouts, and configured thresholds. A request already sent can still fail.

beats.text: The balancer sends a health probe.
A is excluded from new selection.
A new request routes to B.
B returns its response through the balancer.
